opus-5.5.text:
I think we're starting to see inference providers specialize around a few distinct workload patterns, rather than one generic "serve the model" offering.

The first is the low-latency, interactive case: chatbots, coding assistants, anything where a human is waiting on the other end. There, what matters is time to first token and tokens per second per user. Providers optimize for that with things like speculative decoding, smaller batch sizes, and very careful kernel work so you're not leaving memory bandwidth on the table during decode. Some are even willing to pay more per token in hardware efficiency because users will pay a premium for speed.

The second is high-throughput batch workloads: synthetic data generation, evals, offline document processing. Latency barely matters; cost per token is everything. You can run huge batch sizes, pack requests aggressively, and use cheaper or older hardware. That's why you see batch APIs at roughly half price. The economics are just different.

The third, which I think is growing fastest, is agentic workloads. These look quite different: very long contexts, lots of repeated prefixes, many sequential calls, tool use in between. So prefix caching and KV cache management become first-class concerns. If an agent sends the same 50,000-token context fifty times with small changes, reusing that cache is the difference between a viable product and an unaffordable one. You also see people separating prefill from decode onto different hardware, since prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bound, and long-context agentic work stresses them very differently.

On the architecture side, this is part of why I'm excited about things like state-space models and hybrid architectures. A fixed-size state instead of a growing KV cache changes the inference economics for long-context and agentic use. Model design and inference systems are increasingly being co-designed around the workload.

So I expect more fragmentation. Different providers, or different tiers within the same provider, will be tuned for speed, for cost, or for long-context agentic serving. The ones who understand their customers' workload shape best will have a real edge, because there's no single configuration that's optimal for everything.

r001.rationale: The response groups chatbots with low-latency interactive workloads and emphasizes speed and premium responsiveness; it does not characterize traditional chatbot workloads as requiring moderate responsiveness.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the interesting thing is that inference is no longer one problem. A year or two ago, everyone was basically serving the same shape of request: a chat prompt comes in, maybe a few hundred tokens, you decode a few hundred tokens back, done. And you could optimize for that one regime. Now the workloads have really diverged.

On one end you have these very long context, mostly prefill-heavy workloads. Think about coding agents dumping an entire repository into context, or document understanding, or RAG with a lot of retrieved material. There the bottleneck is compute. You're doing big matrix multiplies over tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens, and the question is how efficiently you can keep the tensor cores busy, how you do things like chunked prefill, prefix caching, so you're not recomputing the same system prompt or the same codebase over and over.

On the other end you have the agentic and reasoning workloads, where the model might generate ten, twenty, fifty thousand tokens of chain of thought or tool calls before it produces something the user actually sees. That's decode-dominated, and decode is memory-bandwidth bound. Every step you're reading the weights and the KV cache off HBM, and you're generating one token per sequence. So there the game is completely different. It's about batching, it's about how small you can make the KV cache, which is why you see a lot of interest in things like MLA or GQA or quantizing the cache, and it's about speculative decoding, where you try to get more than one token per forward pass.

So what I see providers doing is, first, disaggregation. Running prefill and decode on different sets of GPUs, because the hardware you want for each is actually different. Prefill wants a lot of FLOPs, decode wants a lot of bandwidth and ideally a lot of memory to hold big batches. And once you separate them you can scale them independently depending on what the traffic mix looks like that hour.

Second, they're getting much smarter about scheduling. If you have a latency-sensitive interactive request and a batch job that can tolerate being slow, you don't want them in the same queue competing for the same batch slots. So you see tiered offerings, batch APIs that are much cheaper, priority queues, and the scheduler is making those tradeoffs explicitly.

And third, I think the hardware itself is starting to specialize. People are talking about chips that are basically designed for decode, with huge SRAM or very high bandwidth, versus chips that are good at the dense compute for prefill or for training. For a long time the answer was just "buy the latest NVIDIA GPU and run everything on it," and that's still mostly true, but the economics are now big enough that specializing starts to make sense.

From my side, on the kernel and systems level, what this means is you can't just have one attention kernel anymore. You need a prefill kernel, a decode kernel, something for the speculative case where you're verifying a few tokens at once, something for very long sequences where you split the KV across many devices. A lot of the work in FlashAttention 3 and what we've been doing since then is really about covering all of those regimes well on the same hardware, because the providers need all of them simultaneously.

r001.rationale: The response describes traditional chat requests as a few hundred prompt and output tokens, but does not characterize their inference responsiveness as moderate.

astra-6.text:
I think inference providers will have to specialize more around the workload. If you’re serving an interactive application, you care a lot about latency—how quickly you get the first token and how quickly subsequent tokens arrive. If you’re processing a large batch of documents overnight, you’re probably willing to wait longer if the cost is lower. Those workloads call for different choices around batching, scheduling, and hardware utilization.

Even within one request, processing the prompt and generating the response have different computational characteristics. So there’s an opportunity to allocate resources differently for those phases, rather than treating inference as one uniform operation.

I’d expect providers to offer more explicit tradeoffs: here’s a low-latency service, here’s a throughput-oriented service, and here’s what each costs. The interesting systems problem is how much of that adaptation you can do automatically as the traffic changes.

r001.rationale: The response says interactive applications care a lot about latency, but it does not characterize traditional chatbot workloads or describe their responsiveness as moderate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think inference is going to become much more specialized around the workload. If you’re serving a chatbot, you care a lot about latency—how quickly the first token comes back and how fast the subsequent tokens arrive. If you’re processing a million documents overnight, you care much more about throughput and cost. You can tolerate waiting, especially if that lets the provider batch requests more efficiently.

Even within one request, the computational pattern changes. Processing the input—the prefill phase—is quite different from generating tokens one at a time. So I think we’ll see providers separate those phases more, and choose different hardware and scheduling policies for each.

The interesting challenge is that the traffic isn’t static. Input lengths change, output lengths change, and demand comes in bursts. Having a fast kernel is important, but you also need a system that can keep the hardware busy while meeting the latency target. I’d expect providers to offer more explicit tradeoffs: here’s the low-latency service, here’s the cheaper batch service, and here’s what you pay for each.

r001.rationale: The response says chatbot serving cares a lot about latency and emphasizes quick token delivery. It does not characterize traditional chatbot responsiveness as moderate.
